passageText: Allan Houser created contemporary Apache sculpture. As a child, he listened to his father's stories about the adventures of Chief Geronimo. This gave him a deep attachment to his ancestral background, an attachment that is shown in his artwork. Houser studied at the Indian School in Santa Fe, New Mexico, and then remained in Santa Fe, where he worked as a freelance artist. During World War II, he traveled to California, where he became interested in the media of sculpture. He created works in a variety of styles and mastered bronze, metal, and stone sculpture. Houser's designs are modern, yet firmly rooted in the special tradition of his Native American forefathers. He drew inspiration from both past and present, but like all successful artists, his sculpture transcends race and language. The sculpture Reverie shows a distinct Native American influence, but it can be appreciated by anyone, regardless of his or her background.

answer.surroundingText: Next time you look up, you'll see someone else similarly immersed, and you won't feel alone at all. Reading can be sociable.

answerStage.explanation: 지각동사 see의 목적격 보어 자리의 능동과 수동 관계를 묻는 문항입니다. 목적어인 someone else(다른 누군가)가 무언가를 능동적으로 몰입시키고 있는 것이 아니라, 책 속의 세계 등에 의해 '몰입되어 있는' 상태를 나타내야 하므로 과거분사인 immersed를 쓰는 것이 옳습니다. 따라서 현재분사형인 immersing은 문법적으로 부적절합니다.

question.passageWithMarkers: We all enjoy the pleasure of __(A) being left__ alone with a good book. But sometimes after several hours of immersion we lift our heads and look around, suddenly struck by the quiet, the absence of others. In this situation, we are suffering from reading-induced loneliness. The solution is to read in the company of other people __(B) who__ are reading - whether in a public space such as a café or a library, or in your own home, with your reading friend or partner at the other end of the sofa. Next time you look up, you'll see someone else similarly __(C) immersing__, and you won't feel alone at all. Reading can be sociable. Consider joining a reading group __(D) in which__ everybody takes turns reading aloud from a novel. Reading a book collaboratively __(E) is__ a wonderful way to share an otherwise internal and solitary experience.

passageText: We all enjoy the pleasure of being left alone with a good book. But sometimes after several hours of immersion we lift our heads and look around, suddenly struck by the quiet, the absence of others. In this situation, we are suffering from reading-induced loneliness. The solution is to read in the company of other people who are reading - whether in a public space such as a café or a library, or in your own home, with your reading friend or partner at the other end of the sofa. Next time you look up, you'll see someone else similarly immersed, and you won't feel alone at all. Reading can be sociable. Consider joining a reading group in which everybody takes turns reading aloud from a novel. Reading a book collaboratively is a wonderful way to share an otherwise internal and solitary experience.

question.passageWithMarkers: We tend to think of technology as shiny tools and gadgets. Even if we acknowledge that technology can exist in disembodied form, __(A) such as__ software, we tend not to include in this category paintings, literature, music, dance, poetry, and the arts in general. But we should. If a thousand lines of letters in UNIX __(B) qualifies__ as a technology (the computer code for a web page), then a thousand lines of letters in English (Hamlet) must qualify as well. A Shakespeare sonnet and a Schubert symphony, then, are in the same category as Google's search engine and the smartphone: They are something useful __(C) produced__ by a mind. We can't separate out the multiple overlapping technologies __(D) responsible__ for a Lord of the Rings movie. The literary rendering of the original novel __(E) are__ as much an invention as the digital rendering of its fantastical creatures. Both are useful works of the human imagination. Both influence audiences powerfully. Both are technological.

passageText: We tend to think of technology as shiny tools and gadgets. Even if we acknowledge that technology can exist in disembodied form, such as software, we tend not to include in this category paintings, literature, music, dance, poetry, and the arts in general. But we should. If a thousand lines of letters in UNIX qualifies as a technology (the computer code for a web page), then a thousand lines of letters in English (Hamlet) must qualify as well. They both can change our behavior, alter the course of events, or enable future inventions. A Shakespeare sonnet and a Schubert symphony, then, are in the same category as Google's search engine and the smartphone: They are something useful produced by a mind. We can't separate out the multiple overlapping technologies responsible for a Lord of the Rings movie. The literary rendering of the original novel is as much an invention as the digital rendering of its fantastical creatures. Both are useful works of the human imagination. Both influence audiences powerfully. Both are technological.

passageText: When we see something, we naturally and automatically break it up into shapes, colors, and concepts that we have learned through education. We recode what we see through the lens of everything we know. We reconstruct memories rather than retrieving the video from memory. This is a useful trait. It's a more efficient way to store information - a bit like an optimal image compression algorithm such as JPG, rather than storing a raw bitmap image file. The discovery that our memories are reconstructed through abstract representations rather than played back like a movie completely undermined the legal primacy of eyewitness testimony. Seeing is not believing.

passageText: We tend to go long periods of time without reaching out to the people we know. Then, we suddenly take notice of the distance that has formed and we scramble to make repairs. passageText: Unfortunately, many people don't take personal responsibility for their own growth. Instead, they simply run the race laid out for them. They do well enough in school to keep advancing. passageText: A lovely technique for helping children take the first steps towards creating their own, unique story, is to ask them to help you complete a story before you tell it. passageText: Whether or not we can catch up on sleep - on the weekend, say - is a hotly debated topic among sleep researchers; the latest evidence suggests that while it isn't ideal, it might help. When Peter Liu, a UCLA sleep researcher, brought chronically sleep-restricted people into the lab for a weekend of sleep during which they slept about 10 hours per night, they showed improvements in the ability of insulin to process blood sugar. That suggests that catch-up sleep may undo some but not all of the damage that sleep deprivation causes, which is encouraging given how many adults don't get the hours they need each night. Still, Liu isn't ready to endorse the habit of sleeping less and making up for it later. "It's like telling people you only need to eat healthy during the weekends, but during the week you can eat whatever you like," he says.

answerStage.explanation: 이 문장은 단어 선택에 대한 권고를 나타내는 명령문입니다. 'Choose'로 시작하는 문장에서 주절을 이끌 정동사가 반드시 필요하지만, 이를 'Choosing'이라는 분사(준동사)로 바꾸면 문장 전체를 완결할 동사가 사라지게 됩니다. 'that are more expressive'는 words를 수식하는 관계사절이고, 'if' 이하는 조건의 부사절일 뿐입니다. 따라서 문장의 뼈대를 구성하는 정동사 원형인 Choose로 고쳐야 올바른 문장이 됩니다.

wrongOptionExplanations.(B): thought of 뒤의 전치사 목적어가 빠진 불완전한 절을 이끌며 asked의 직접 목적어 역할을 하는 명사절로 사용된 what은 적절합니다.

question.explanation: 문장의 골격을 살펴보면 단어를 선택하라고 권고하는 내용입니다. 밑줄 친 표현인 Choosing부터 문장 끝까지 살펴보았을 때, 이 문장을 이끄는 정동사가 존재하지 않습니다. 따라서 Choosing이라는 현재분사가 위치하는 것은 비문이 됩니다. 문장이 정상적으로 성립하려면 주절의 역할을 하는 정동사인 명령문 동사원형 형태 Choose로 고쳐야 합니다. 주어를 수식하는 분사구문으로 착각할 수 있으나 정동사가 없으므로 불가능합니다.
keyPoints: (D) 명령문과 정동사 — 조건 부사절 및 수식어구를 제외한 주절에 정동사가 요구됨
(B) 명사절 접속사 what — 뒤에 불완전한 문장이 오고 명사 역할을 함
(C) to부정사의 부사적 용법 — ~하기 위해서를 의미하며 동사를 수식함

passageText: Some of the words we use most frequently are not expressive. If someone asked you what you thought of a movie or your dinner, you might respond: "It was fine." Do you mean, 'fine' as in 'fine wine,' or 'fine art?' Or do you mean, 'fine' as in 'excellent, good, fine or poor?' 'Fine' can be used to express satisfaction or disappointment. Choose words that are more expressive, like 'great' or 'terrific' or 'wonderful' if you want to express pleasure, and words like 'adequate' or 'satisfactory' if your intent is to communicate that the movie or meal was okay, but nothing more. answerStage.direction: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?

'so'절이 뒤따르지만, 이는 목적을 나타내는 부사절일 뿐 앞의 주절 동사 구조와는 독립적이므로 반증 검사 시에도 여전히 비문입니다.

answer.surroundingText: He took pity on the people, gave them bendable knees and cutting off their inconvenient kangaroo tails so they could all sit down at last.

answerStage.explanation: 문장의 주어인 He에 연결되는 동사들이 process(과거형 동사)로 병렬되고 있습니다. 문맥상 '불쌍히 여겼고(took), 무릎을 주었으며(gave), 꼬리를 잘랐다(cut)'라는 세 가지 동작이 대등하게 연결되어야 합니다. 따라서 등위접속사 and 뒤에는 준동사인 cutting이 아니라, 앞서 나온 took, gave와 시제를 일치시킨 과거동사 cut이 와야 어법상 적절합니다.

question.direction: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?

markedExpressions.label: (A)
markedExpressions.surroundingText: Moinee fell out of the stars down to Tasmania to die.

markedExpressions.label: (B)
markedExpressions.surroundingText: But he was in such a hurry, knowing he was dying, that he forgot to give them knees;

markedExpressions.label: (C)
markedExpressions.surroundingText: gave them big tails like kangaroos, which meant they couldn't sit down. Then he died.

markedExpressions.label: (D)
markedExpressions.surroundingText: He took pity on the people, gave them bendable knees and cutting off their inconvenient kangaroo tails so they could all sit down at last.

markedExpressions.label: (E)
markedExpressions.surroundingText: Then they lived happily ever after.

wrongOptionExplanations.(A): 문장의 주어 Moinee에 이어지는 본동사 자리이므로 과거형 동사 fell은 적절합니다.
wrongOptionExplanations.(B): 주어인 he가 죽어가고 있다는 사실을 능동적으로 인지하고 있는 상태를 나타내므로 현재분사 knowing은 적절합니다.
wrongOptionExplanations.(C): 앞 문장 전체를 선행사로 받아 부연 설명을 이어가는 관계대명사의 계속적 용법으로 which는 적절합니다.
wrongOptionExplanations.(E): 동사 lived를 수식하며 '행복하게 살았다'라는 의미를 완성하는 부사 자리이므로 happily는 적절합니다.

question.explanation: 문장의 주어인 He에 연결되는 세 가지 동작이 and를 통해 병렬 구조를 이루고 있습니다. took(불쌍히 여겼고), gave(무릎을 주었으며)와 함께 문맥상 '꼬리를 잘랐다'라는 동작이 대등하게 이어져야 하므로, 준동사인 cutting을 앞선 과거동사들과 시제를 일치시킨 과거동사 cut으로 고쳐야 합니다. 'cutting off'를 분사구문으로 오해할 수 있으나, 등위접속사 and가 이미 존재하므로 동사가 나열되는 구조로 파악하는 것이 타당합니다.
keyPoints: (D) 병렬 구조 — 등위접속사 and로 연결되는 동사의 형태 일치 여부 확인
(B) 분사의 능동과 수동 — 생략된 주어와의 능동적 의미 강도를 통한 현재분사 선택
(C) 관계대명사 — 계속적 용법의 which가 이끄는 절의 완전성 및 기능 판단
question.passageWithMarkers: A god called Moinee was defeated by a rival god called Dromerdeener in a terrible battle up in the stars. Moinee __(A) fell__ out of the stars down to Tasmania to die. Before he died, he wanted to give a last blessing to his final resting place, so he decided to create humans. But he was in such a hurry, __(B) knowing__ he was dying, that he forgot to give them knees; and he absent-mindedly gave them big tails like kangaroos, __(C) which__ meant they couldn't sit down. Then he died. The people hated having kangaroo tails and no knees, and they cried out to the heavens for help. Dromerdeener heard their cry and came down to Tasmania to see what the matter was. He took pity on the people, gave them bendable knees and __(D) cutting__ off their inconvenient kangaroo tails so they could all sit down at last. Then they lived __(E) happily__ ever after.

passageText: A god called Moinee was defeated by a rival god called Dromerdeener in a terrible battle up in the stars. Moinee fell out of the stars down to Tasmania to die. Before he died, he wanted to give a last blessing to his final resting place, so he decided to create humans. But he was in such a hurry, knowing he was dying, that he forgot to give them knees; and he absent-mindedly gave them big tails like kangaroos, which meant they couldn't sit down. Then he died. The people hated having kangaroo tails and no knees, and they cried out to the heavens for help. Dromerdeener heard their cry and came down to Tasmania to see what the matter was. He took pity on the people, gave them bendable knees and cut off their inconvenient kangaroo tails so they could all sit down at last. Then they lived happily ever after.

answerStage.direction: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
answerStage.answerDesign: 정답 문장은 'A remark may be made to cause your anger, but responding with a cool answer that focuses on the issue raised is likely to be most effective.'입니다. 동명사구 주어인 'responding ~ raised'의 서술어 자리에 있는 단수 동사 'is'를 'are'로 변형하여 수일치 오류를 생성합니다. 문장의 주어 핵이 수식어구에 가려져 멀리 떨어져 있으므로 구조적 분석이 요구되는 자리입니다. 반증 검사 결과, 등위접속사 but 뒤에 이어지는 절의 주어가 동명사구이므로 복수형 동사 are는 문법적으로 성립할 수 없습니다.

answer.surroundingText: A remark may be made to cause your anger, but responding with a cool answer that focuses on the issue raised is likely to be most effective.

answerStage.explanation: 등위접속사 but 뒤의 절에서 주어는 'responding with a cool answer that focuses on the issue raised'라는 동명사구입니다. 동명사구 주어는 문법적으로 단수 취급을 원칙으로 하므로, 복수 비동사인 are를 단수 형태인 is로 고쳐야 합니다. 주어구 내에 위치한 명사 issue 등에 현혹되지 않고 전체 문장의 술어 동사 구조를 파악하는 것이 중요합니다.

question.direction: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?

markedExpressions.label: (A)
markedExpressions.surroundingText: We all know that tempers are one of the first things lost in many arguments.

markedExpressions.label: (B)
markedExpressions.surroundingText: the other person is trying to get you to be angry.

markedExpressions.label: (C)
markedExpressions.surroundingText: They may be saying things that are intentionally designed to annoy you.

markedExpressions.label: (D)
markedExpressions.surroundingText: you'll say something that sounds foolish; you'll simply get angry

markedExpressions.label: (E)
markedExpressions.surroundingText: Indeed, any attentive listener will admire the fact that you didn't "rise to the bait."

wrongOptionExplanations.(A): 명사구 'the first things'를 뒤에서 수식하는 과거분사 lost입니다. things가 '잃어버려지는' 수동의 관계이므로 과거분사 형용사구가 적절히 쓰였습니다.
wrongOptionExplanations.(B): get은 5형식 문장에서 목적격 보어로 to부정사를 취하는 동사입니다. 목적어인 you가 화가 나는(to be) 상황을 유도한다는 의미이므로 to get과 호응하는 to be는 어법상 옳습니다.
wrongOptionExplanations.(C): 과거분사(형용사 역할)인 designed를 수식하는 부사 자리입니다. '의도적으로 설계된'이라는 의미를 구성하며 분사를 꾸미기 위해 intentionally를 사용한 것은 적절합니다.
wrongOptionExplanations.(D): 선행사 something을 수식하고 뒤에 바로 동사 sounds가 이어지는 것으로 보아, 주격 관계대명사 that이 올바르게 사용되었습니다.

question.explanation: 문장의 목적어 역할을 하는 명사구 'the fact' 뒤에 위치하여 이를 구체적으로 부연 설명하는 동격절 자리입니다. 이어지는 절인 'you didn't rise to the bait'가 주어와 동사, 수식어구까지 모두 갖춘 완전한 구조이므로, 명사 역할을 완벽한 절과 연결해 줄 수 있는 동격의 접속사가 와야 합니다. 관계대명사는 불완전한 구조의 절을 이끌어야 하므로, 제시된 문맥과 구조 내에서는 비문이 됩니다. 따라서 틀린 표현 which를 완전한 절을 연결하는 접속사 that으로 고쳐야 합니다. 학생들이 관계대명사와 유사하게 생긴 명사절 접속사를 단순 관계사로 착각하기 쉽습니다.
keyPoints: (E) 동격 접속사 vs 관계대명사 — 이어지는 절의 완전성으로 판정
(A) 분사의 능동 vs 수동 — 명사와의 의미 관계에 따라 과거분사로 수식함
(B) 목적격 보어의 형태 — get + 목적어 + to-v 구문에서의 형태 판단
question.passageWithMarkers: We all know that tempers are one of the first things __(A) lost__ in many arguments. It's easy to say one should keep cool, but how do you do it? The point to remember is that sometimes in arguments the other person is trying __(B) to get__ you to be angry. They may be saying things that are __(C) intentionally__ designed to annoy you. They know that if they get you to lose your cool you'll say something __(D) that__ sounds foolish; you'll simply get angry and then it will be impossible for you to win the argument. So don't fall for it. A remark may be made to cause your anger, but responding with a cool answer that focuses on the issue raised is likely to be most effective. Indeed, any attentive listener will admire the fact __(E) which__ you didn't "rise to the bait."

passageText: We all know that tempers are one of the first things lost in many arguments. It's easy to say one should keep cool, but how do you do it? The point to remember is that sometimes in arguments the other person is trying to get you to be angry. They may be saying things that are intentionally designed to annoy you. They know that if they get you to lose your cool you'll say something that sounds foolish; you'll simply get angry and then it will be impossible for you to win the argument. So don't fall for it. A remark may be made to cause your anger, but responding with a cool answer that focuses on the issue raised is likely to be most effective. Indeed, any attentive listener will admire the fact that you didn't "rise to the bait."

answerStage.direction: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
answerStage.answerDesign: 문장 'When we try to comfort a child with food rather than attend to their physical and emotional needs, we leave them feeling not understood.'에서 5형식 동사 leave 뒤의 목적격 보어 자리에 쓰인 'feeling'을 'feel'로 변형합니다. leave는 목적격 보어로 현재분사(v-ing)나 형용사를 취하여 '목적어가 ~한 상태로 두다'라는 의미를 형성하므로, 동사 원형인 feel은 이 자리에 올 수 없는 통사적 비문입니다. 지각동사나 사역동사가 아니므로 원형 부정사는 허용되지 않으며, 문맥상 아이가 느끼는 '상태'를 묘사해야 하므로 형용사적 성격의 분사가 반드시 필요합니다.

answer.surroundingText: When we try to comfort a child with food rather than attend to their physical and emotional needs, we leave them feeling not understood.

passageText: Giving kids an edible treat that you know they love after a tricky day to cheer them up or soothe them can be tempting but I advise you not to. passageText: We say to ourselves: “There is plenty of time. I’ll manage somehow or other when the time comes for action.” We are rather proud of our ability to meet emergencies. So we do not plan and take precautions to prevent emergencies from arising. It is too easy to drift through school and college, taking the traditional, conventional studies that others take, following the lines of least resistance, electing “snap courses,” and going with the crowd. It is too easy to take the attitude: “First I will get my education and develop myself, and then I will know better what I am fitted to do for a life work.” And so we drift, driven by the winds of circumstance, tossed about by the waves of tradition and custom. Eventually, most men find they must be satisfied with “any port in a storm.” Sailors who select a port because they are driven to it have scarcely one chance in a thousand of dropping anchor in the right one.

passageText: Here's an interesting thought. If glaciers started re-forming, they have a great deal more water now to draw on ― Hudson Bay, the Great Lakes, the hundreds of thousands of lakes of Canada, none of which existed to fuel the last ice sheet ― so they would grow very much quicker. And if they did start to advance again, what exactly would we do? Blast them with TNT or maybe nuclear missiles? Well, doubtless we would, but consider this. In 1964, the largest earthquake ever recorded in North America rocked Alaska with 200,000 megatons of concentrated might, the equivalent of 2,000 nuclear bombs. Almost 3,000 miles away in Texas, water sloshed out of swimming pools. A street in Anchorage fell twenty feet. The quake devastated 24,000 square miles of wilderness, much of it glaciated. And what effect did all this might have on Alaska's glaciers? None.
